client: I've been feeling really anxious and insecure about my new job ever since my coworker called me out in front of everyone during last week's team meeting. I keep replaying that moment in my head and now I'm second-guessing everything I do, worrying I'll mess up again. Part of me wonders if talking about it will help, because the problem feels so real - like maybe I'm just not cut out for this role.
therapist: It sounds like that moment really shook your confidence, and I can hear both the hurt and hesitation in your voice as you share this. Let's examine that thought about not being cut out for this role - what evidence do you have that contradicts that belief? The fact that you care this much actually suggests you're quite invested in doing well.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess my manager did say I was doing fine in my one-on-one last month... But that was before this incident happened. It just feels like all my past mistakes are piling up now, and I keep imagining worst-case scenarios where I get fired. Logically I know one bad moment doesn't define me, but emotionally it's hard to shake this feeling.
therapist: Your voice sounds really tense as you describe this - I can hear how much these anxious thoughts are racing for you right now. That gap between knowing something logically and feeling it emotionally is completely normal, and we can work through those worst-case scenarios to see if they hold up under closer examination.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I know we're supposed to examine those worst-case thoughts, but they feel so real in the moment. Like when I'm about to speak in a meeting now, my mind just floods with "What if I say something stupid again?" or "Everyone's probably just waiting for me to mess up." It's exhausting.
therapist: I can hear the frustration and exhaustion in your voice as you describe how these anxious thoughts take over - they really do feel overwhelming when they flood in like that. Let's slow down for a moment: when you notice those "what if" thoughts coming up, what's one small piece of evidence that contradicts them? Maybe someone's nod or attentive look during a meeting?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Hmm... I guess my teammate did ask for my input on a project yesterday. But then my brain says that's just because they had to, not because they actually value what I think. I wish I could just take the positive moments at face value instead of always finding ways to discount them.
therapist: There's a hopeful shift in your tone as you mention your teammate reaching out - that's progress worth recognizing. Let's challenge that automatic thought about them "having to" ask you - what would it mean if we took this as evidence that your contributions are actually valued?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I never thought about it that way... I mean, if they didn't value my input, they probably wouldn't have asked at all, right? But it's still hard because part of me is waiting for the other shoe to drop. What if they're just being nice until they get tired of me failing?
therapist: Your voice sounds anxious as you share this, and I can hear how that fear of future rejection is still lingering despite this new perspective. That "waiting for the other shoe to drop" feeling is so common with anxiety - let's explore how we might challenge that anticipation of failure with concrete examples of when things actually went okay.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I can think of a few small wins - like when I caught that error in the report last week. But my brain immediately counters that with "one right doesn't cancel out all the wrongs." It's like I'm keeping this mental tally that's always weighted against me. Why does the negative stuff always seem to count more?
therapist: I can hear both the frustration and the quickening pace in your voice as you describe this mental tally - it's exhausting to feel like you're constantly battling against yourself. That tendency to weigh negatives more heavily is actually our brain's built-in negativity bias at work, not a true reflection of your actual performance. Let's look at how we might consciously balance that scale when you notice it tipping.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I get what you're saying about negativity bias, but how do I actually change it? Every time I try to focus on positives, it feels forced and fake, like I'm just lying to myself. Maybe some people are just wired to see the glass half empty.
therapist: I hear the skepticism and frustration in your voice - this feels like an uphill battle right now. Let's reframe it: instead of trying to "force" positivity, what if we simply notice when your brain discounts good things, and gently ask "Is that necessarily true?" No pressure to believe it yet, just creating space for alternative possibilities.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: That approach actually sounds less overwhelming than trying to force myself to be positive. But I worry I'll just get stuck in endless questioning - like when I try to challenge a negative thought, my anxiety just comes up with ten more reasons why it's true. How do I know when to stop analyzing and just accept a more balanced view?
therapist: I can hear the anxious energy in your quick speech as you describe this worry about endless questioning - it makes sense that this process would feel exhausting right now. Instead of seeing it as an all-or-nothing choice between overanalyzing or accepting, let's explore how to recognize when you've gathered enough evidence to reasonably challenge that initial anxious thought.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I don't know how to recognize that point though - my brain always wants more certainty than exists. Like even if I list three good things that happened, my anxiety says "But what about tomorrow?" Maybe I'm just not the type of person who can do this kind of mental reframing. It all feels so fuzzy compared to the concrete certainty of my fears.
therapist: Your voice sounds both hesitant and thoughtful as you explain this struggle - I can hear how the uncertainty feels so uncomfortable compared to anxiety's false sense of concrete certainty. Let's acknowledge that this reframing process does feel fuzzy at first, like learning a new language - it's okay if it doesn't click immediately, and we can work on recognizing progress in small steps rather than expecting perfection.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I can try taking smaller steps... But part of me still worries I'll never fully "get" this way of thinking. How will I know if I'm making real progress versus just going through the motions? It all still feels abstract compared to the very real pit in my stomach when I walk into the office.
therapist: I can hear both the uncertainty and the anxious energy in your quick, higher-pitched speech - that physical discomfort when you walk into the office feels so immediate and real. Let's look for concrete signs of progress, like moments when that pit in your stomach feels slightly less intense, or when you're able to notice an anxious thought without completely believing it.
